Abnormal Labour & Obstetric Emergencies

Abnormal labour and obstetric emergencies — obstructed labour, malpresentation, cord prolapse, rupture, shock and post-partum haemorrhage.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Recognise obstructed labour
  • Manage cord prolapse and shoulder dystocia
  • Describe rupture of uterus
  • Manage postpartum haemorrhage and shock

In simple words

Abnormal labour is labour where the baby cannot be delivered naturally without danger. Early recognition and timely referral save both lives.

Abnormal labour — causes

Cause Example
Passenger Malpresentation (breech, transverse, face), macrosomia, fetal abnormality
Passage Contracted pelvis, full bladder, cervical fibrosis
Power Weak or incoordinate contractions
Psyche Fear, exhaustion

Signs of obstructed labour

  • Slow progress of cervical dilatation despite good contractions
  • Head does not descend; moulding and caput
  • Bandl’s ring, continuous pain, fetal distress
  • Maternal exhaustion, tachycardia, dehydration
  • Uterus may rupture if unrelieved

Cord prolapse and shoulder dystocia

Cord prolapse: sudden fetal distress with a palpable pulseless cord. Kneel-elbow position, lift the presenting part by hand, give oxygen, and deliver immediately by the fastest route.

Shoulder dystocia: head delivers but shoulders are stuck. Deliver the anterior arm, use McRoberts manoeuvre and apply suprapubic pressure.

Rupture of the uterus

  • Sudden severe abdominal pain, haemorrhage, shock, absent fetal heart, easily palpable fetal parts
  • Immediate laparotomy and resuscitation

Postpartum haemorrhage

Causes (4 Ts): Tone (atony — commonest), Tissue (retained products), Trauma (tears), Thrombin (clotting failure).

Management: call for help, rub the uterus, give oxytocic, check for tears and retained products, compress the aorta, fluids and blood.

🔴 Obstructed labour must not be allowed to become rupture

Signs such as non-descent, constant pain and maternal exhaustion demand urgent obstetric referral. A timely caesarean or operative delivery is the only safe plan.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Causes of abnormal labour: passenger, passage, power, psyche.
  2. Obstructed labour shows slow progress with non-descent and constant pain.
  3. In cord prolapse, relieve pressure and deliver immediately.
  4. Rupture of the uterus causes shock, severe pain and absent fetal heart.
  5. 4 Ts of postpartum haemorrhage: tone, tissue, trauma, thrombin.
  6. First treatment of uterine atony is uterine massage plus oxytocics.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Prolonged labour is more than 12 hours in the first stage.
  2. McRoberts and suprapubic pressure are used for shoulder dystocia.
  3. Retained placenta needs manual removal.
  4. Hypovolaemic shock needs fast crystalloid and blood.
  5. Prevention of PPH begins with active management of the third stage.

📌 Memory trick

PPH: 4 Ts — Tone, Tissue, Trauma, Thrombin.

60-second revision

  • Abnormal labour is due to the passenger, passage, power or psyche.
  • Obstructed labour: slow progress, non-descent, constant pain, exhaustion.
  • Cord prolapse: relieve the pressure and deliver fast.
  • Rupture: sudden pain, shock, absent fetal heart — laparotomy.
  • PPH causes: tone, tissue, trauma, thrombin; treat with massage, oxytocics, fluids.

Test yourself

The commonest cause of postpartum haemorrhage is:

Answer: A. Uterine atony (failure to contract) is the commonest cause of PPH.

In cord prolapse, the nurse should:

Answer: B. The nurse relieves pressure by the presenting part and arranges the fastest delivery.

Which is a sign of obstructed labour?

Answer: A. Non-descent and slow progress despite good contractions indicate obstructed labour.

Rupture of the uterus is suspected when there is:

Answer: B. Sudden severe pain, haemorrhage and shock with absent fetal heart suggest uterine rupture.

Uterine atony is treated first by:

Answer: B. Massage and uterotonic drugs are the immediate treatment for uterine atony.
